slides.title: Introduction to Data Types
slides.content: C# is a statically typed language, meaning every variable must have a declared type. Common types include int for integers, double for decimals, bool for true/false, string for text, and char for single characters.
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Which keyword declares a variable that can hold 'Hello'?

slides.title: Numeric Types
slides.content: C# provides several numeric types. int stores 32-bit whole numbers, double stores 64-bit floating-point numbers, and decimal is used for financial calculations requiring high precision.
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: What keyword declares a 64-bit floating-point number?

slides.title: Boolean Type
slides.content: The bool type represents truth values and can only be true or false. It is commonly used in conditional statements and loops.
slides.exampleOutput: No output: the shown condition is false.

exercise.prompt: What is the default value of an uninitialized bool variable?

slides.title: String and Char
slides.content: string represents text as a sequence of Unicode characters, while char represents a single Unicode character. Strings use double quotes, and chars use single quotes.
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: Complete the declaration of a char variable.

slides.title: Type Sizes and Ranges
slides.content: Each C# type has a fixed size regardless of platform. int is 4 bytes, double is 8 bytes, and char is 2 bytes. You can use sizeof(int) to verify sizes at compile time.

exercise.prompt: How many bytes does a char use?

slides.title: Default Values
slides.content: In C#, fields (class-level variables) are automatically initialized to default values: numeric types to 0, bool to false, char to '\0', and reference types like string to null.
slides.exampleOutput: Class definition; produces no console output.

exercise.prompt: What is the default value of an uninitialized string field?

slides.title: Declaring Variables
slides.content: Use the var keyword for implicit typing when the compiler can infer the type from the initializer. You can also declare multiple variables of the same type in one statement.
slides.exampleOutput: Declaration or expression only; produces no console output.

slides.title: Practice: Data Types
slides.content: Combine what you learned: declare variables of different types, understand their defaults, and print them. This prepares you for type casting and user input.
